catalog_quote: ACENTO El acento generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. (Una excepción es la palabra /ɑˈri/ ‘sí’.) Por lo tanto, cuando se añade un sufijo, el acento cambia de sílaba: /ˈmɑki/ ‘mano’, /mɑkinˈkunɑ/ ‘sus manos’, /ˈkɑʒbɑj/ ‘corre’, /kɑʒbɑˈɾɑjki/ ‘corriste’, /kɑʒbɑnɢɑˈʒɑpɑ/ ‘correrán’. PALABRA MÍNIMA Y SÍLABA La palabra mínima generalmente tiene dos sílabas si es de clase léxica mayor. Excepciones son: /ˈnɑn/ ‘camino’, /ˈnij/ ‘¡dile! o ¡dí!’, /ˈtɑn/ ‘se sienta’, y /ˈtɑj/ ‘siéntate’. El molde para la sílaba máxima es CVC (con algunas excepciones), y el ataque es obligatorio (excepto en el inicio de la palabra). No hay consonantes extrametricales. Una palabra excepcional con respecto a la estructura silábica de su segunda sílaba es /ɑwˈpɾɑnɑ/ ‘faja de la tejedora’. Palabras con sílabas iniciales especiales son cuatro: /ˈkwiʧkɑ/ ‘demasiado’, /ˈkwɑʃɑ/ ‘triste’, /ˈʧwɑk/ ‘alla’, y /ˈkwɑk/ ‘acá’.

new_statements.translation: STRESS. Stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. (One exception is the word /aˈri/ 'yes'.) Consequently, when a suffix is added the stress changes syllable: /ˈmaki/ 'hand', /makinˈkuna/ 'his/her hands', /ˈkaʒbaj/ 'run!', /kaʒbaˈɾajki/ 'you ran', /kaʒbanɢaˈʒapa/ 'they will run'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word; stress is recomputed after suffixation so it always stays on the penult of the whole word. Lexical exception: ari 'yes' with final stress. The same section notes that the minimal major-class word is disyllabic (with a few monosyllabic exceptions such as /ˈnan/ 'road', /ˈtaj/ 'sit!') and that there are no extrametrical consonants.
new_statements.exceptions: /aˈri/ 'sí' has final stress. Independently, Taylor 1982 (Lexis 6(2): 247) notes that Spanish loans with final stress lose it on nativisation (terrón > tirun 'ha perdido la acentuación aguda'), consistent with penultimate stress; Taylor 1982: 268 also mentions 'modificación acentual' in fused clitic sequences without stating a rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including suffixes); examples are isolated citation forms in phonemic transcription with stress marks. Author is a native speaker from Inkawasi; recordings from Mamajpampa, Quirichima, Atun Loma, Kañaris, Sinchihual and Inkawasi. The 'generalmente' hedge and the preliminary status of the edition should be noted; the more authoritative descriptions (Escribens 1977, Taylor 1996) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Vilcabana Sánchez 2009) describes the Quechua of Inkawasi and Kañaris districts, Ferreñafe province, Lambayeque = lamb1276 (quf) itself; recordings from Mamajpampa, Quirichima, Atun Loma, Kañaris, Sinchihual and Inkawasi. Taylor's work (1982) is based on Ayamachay, Inkawasi district, same language. No dialect-level glottocode distinction needed.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. [...] More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). The northern Peruvian dialects QIIA Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977) and QIIB Amazonas (Taylor 1975; Chaparro 1985) also have deviant stress patterns, as had the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomás.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Vilcabana Sánchez 2009: 'El acento generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba', exception /aˈri/) gives regular penultimate stress. Adelaar 2004:207, second-hand from Escribens 1977 (Fonología del quechua de Ferreñafe), lists QIIA Ferreñafe among the dialects whose stress deviates from the penultimate norm, alongside Ancash, Cajatambo and Amazonas. He gives no rule, so this is a flag of type (not plain fixed: penultimate syllable) rather than an alternative placement; the disagreement can only be settled by reading Escribens 1977 (HathiTrust txu.059173018315742, search-only) or Taylor 1996. Possibly both are reconcilable if Vilcabana's 'generalmente' hides systematic except…
new_statements.rule_in_words: General Quechua: penultimate stress on every polysyllabic word (word-final only in interjections/emphatics). For Ferreñafe (= Lambayeque, QIIA) Quechua specifically, Adelaar states only that it has 'deviant stress patterns' (i.e. not the plain penultimate rule), citing Escribens 1977, without saying where stress falls. No other passage in the book treats Lambayeque/Ferreñafe phonology (the other mentions, pp. 168, 184, 186-188, are classificatory/geographic).
new_statements.exceptions: pan-Quechua: word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw); quantity-insensitive final stress with the first-person long-vowel morpheme; Pacaraos phonemic stress; Ancash/Cajatambo weight- and position-dependent patterns. None specified for Ferreñafe beyond 'deviant'.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the Quechua of the districts of Incahuasi (Inkawasi) and Cañaris (Kañaris), province of Ferreñafe, department of Lambayeque, Peru (Quechua IIA 'Ferreñafe' in Torero/Adelaar's classification = Glottolog lamb1276 Lambayeque Quechua, ISO quf). Vilcabana 2009 calls it 'quechua de Lambayeque'; Adelaar 2004 calls it 'Ferreñafe (Cañaris)'.

readall_conflicts: One flag, no resolved contradiction: the catalog's fixed-penultimate record rests on Vilcabana Sánchez 2009 ('generalmente.. penúltima sílaba', exception /aˈri/ 'sí'), the only primary description read. Adelaar & Muysken 2004:207, citing Escribens 1977, name QIIA Ferreñafe (the same language: Cañaris/Incahuasi, Lambayeque) among Quechua dialects with 'deviant stress patterns', i.e. not the plain penultimate rule, but give no placement. Shaver 1996 (text analysis in Estudios etno-lingüísticos III) could not be opened: the SIL file server answers with an automated-access block and archive.org was unreachable for a the Internet Archive try. The deciding primary sources remain unread: Escribens 1977 Fonología del quechua de Ferreñafe (HathiTrust search-only) and Taylor 1996 El quechua de Ferreñafe.
